name: vtex
_readme: VTEX as a migration TARGET only. Seed from general platform knowledge; everything in research-seed.md is a hypothesis until verified with a developers.vtex.com / help.vtex.com URL and a date. No as_source: VTEX is a multi-tenant SaaS whose extension model is VTEX IO apps and Store Framework blocks - what a client 'has' is app source plus tenant configuration, not an inspectable shop code base with a standard/custom split the scanner can inventory.

as_target.default_frontend: Store Framework (VTEX IO, React block composition) or FastStore for performance-critical headless builds

snippets.critic2_persona: senior solution architect who has delivered VTEX programmes end to end, is VTEX IO certified, and knows the platform's service boundaries (Catalog, Pricing, Logistics, Checkout, OMS, Master Data) and where the IO development model stops - including which capabilities are native, which are VTEX-built apps and which are partner apps
snippets.docs_domains: developers.vtex.com (API reference per service - Catalog, Pricing, Logistics, Checkout, OMS, Master Data, Sessions, Payments - plus VTEX IO app development, Store Framework block reference, FastStore), help.vtex.com (merchant/functional documentation: B2B Suite, promotions, marketplace, OMS operations, franchise accounts), developers.vtex.com/updates and the VTEX release notes for changes, github.com/vtex-apps for the source of the standard apps (the most reliable check for what a block or app actually does). Always name the SERVICE an endpoint belongs to and whether an app is VTEX-maintained or community/partner; the VTEX API surface is service-by-service, not one versioned API.
snippets.best_practice: compose, do not fork: build storefronts from Store Framework blocks and extend through custom IO apps rather than rewriting the standard apps; keep custom data in Master Data v2 entities with an explicit schema rather than in unmanaged fields; treat orderForm as the single source of truth in checkout and add data through orderForm custom apps/attachments rather than side channels; use Intelligent Search rather than raw catalog queries for storefront search; move integration traffic to the order hook and feed rather than polling OMS; keep any per-request external call out of checkout; version and release IO apps through workspaces (dev -> master) with the promotion flow instead of editing production; and model B2B through the B2B Suite apps rather than a bespoke organisation model.
snippets.critic2_focus: D1: which service and which API version a claim belongs to, whether a capability is native, a VTEX-maintained app or a partner app, and its regional availability (several capabilities and payment/logistics integrations are LATAM-first). D2: is the named counterpart a real VTEX service/app (name it) rather than a partner app or project code. D3: does the standard really cover it inside the IO patterns, and is the storefront part available as a Store Framework block or does it need a custom app. D4: exact endpoint paths per service (they differ in pub/pvt scope and authentication), orderForm and OMS data shapes, Master Data schema implications, and whether the required customisation is expressible in the IO model at all.
snippets.expected_hotspots_d3: checkout customisation beyond the sanctioned extension points; complex enterprise B2B (multi-level approval chains, punchout OCI/cXML, contract and quote depth beyond the B2B Suite); ERP-driven customer-specific pricing and availability at request time; configurable products and CPQ; the marketplace-first data model applied to a non-marketplace business (seller, SKU and offer concepts leak into every integration); catalog modelling for deep B2B hierarchies and units of measure; document and content workflow depth; region-specific requirements outside LATAM (tax, payments, logistics, compliance); and reporting/analytics depth.
snippets.expected_blockers_d4: the VTEX IO development model itself - a proprietary app/workspace/block paradigm with a real learning curve and a small experienced talent pool outside LATAM, which is a staffing blocker before it is a technical one; region and partner footprint (strongest in LATAM, still building the enterprise partner network in Europe and North America - check support coverage and reference customers for the project's region); checkout customisation is constrained to the sanctioned extension points, so a heavily customised source checkout does not port; the marketplace-first data model (sellers, offers, split orders, fulfilment vs. marketplace roles) shapes catalog, pricing and OMS even for a single-seller business, and integrations must be designed around it; Master Data v2 is the only place for custom entities and its query/scale characteristics must be validated before it is used as an application database; no self-hosting and no data residency choice; and documentation quality has historically forced reliance on partner knowledge, which is a project risk to plan for.
snippets.content_model_notes: Store Framework is a block composition model, not a page builder in the classic sense: pages are declared in JSON (store/blocks/*.json, store/routes.json) as trees of named blocks - `store.home`, `store.product`, `store.search`, layout blocks (`flex-layout.row`, `flex-layout.col`, `slider-layout`, `tab-layout`, `sticky-layout`, `condition-layout`), and content blocks (`rich-text`, `image`, `info-card`, `product-summary`, `shelf`, `product-price`, `add-to-cart-button`, `minicart`, `search-result-layout`, `breadcrumb`, `menu`). Merchants edit the CONTENT and the props of those blocks in Site Editor (per binding and per page), while the block STRUCTURE lives in the app's JSON and is deployed by developers - so authoring freedom is real but bounded by what the developer exposed. A custom block means a custom React component inside an IO app; nothing renders automatically. Additional content lives in Master Data entities (custom content records), in the legacy CMS/Layout for accounts still on it, and in headless CMS integrations for editorial-heavy sites. FastStore changes the picture again: it is a headless Next.js-based frontend that does not render Store Framework blocks, so a FastStore decision invalidates Store-Framework-level content work. State which frontend a content statement applies to.
